title: Troubleshooting Payment Gateway Timeouts
content: Payment gateway timeouts can occur due to several reasons: 1) Database connection pool exhaustion. 2) Upstream payment processor issues. 3) Network latency. 4) Certificate expiry. Steps: First check the payment service health dashboard. Then review error logs. Common fix: increase DB connection pool or enable failover gateway.
steps: Check payment service health dashboard at monitoring.internal/payment
Review error logs: grep timeout /var/log/payment-service/app.log
Check DB connection pool utilization
Verify payment processor status
Enable failover: set PAYMENT_FAILOVER=true in service config
If unresolved, escalate to #payment-oncall

title: Database Connection Pool Management Best Practices
content: Connection pool exhaustion is a common cause of service outages. Best practices: Set pool size to (num_cores * 2) + num_spindles. Monitor pool utilization via pg_stat_activity. Set connection timeout to avoid indefinite waits. Use PgBouncer for connection multiplexing. Alert when pool utilization exceeds 80%.
steps: Check current pool usage: SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state=active
Review pool configuration in application config file
Increase pool size gradually (e.g., 10 to 25 to 50)
Consider adding PgBouncer as connection proxy
Set up alerting for pool utilization over 80%
Review slow queries that may be holding connections

title: SSL Certificate Monitoring and Renewal Process
content: SSL certificate expiry is a common but preventable outage cause. Set up automated monitoring 90, 30, 14, and 7 days before expiry. Use cert-manager in Kubernetes. Always test certificate renewal in staging first. Keep a runbook for emergency manual renewal.
steps: Check certificate expiry: openssl x509 -enddate -noout -in cert.pem
Verify auto-renewal is configured: systemctl status certbot.timer
Manual renewal: certbot renew --force-renewal
Deploy new certificate to load balancers
Verify with curl -vI https://your-domain.com
Update monitoring alerts for new expiry date

title: Kubernetes OOM Kill Investigation and Resolution
content: When pods are OOM killed, investigate memory growth patterns. Check if there is a memory leak or if resource limits are too low. Use kubectl top to see live usage. Review pod logs before OOM event. Consider Vertical Pod Autoscaler for automatic limit adjustment.
steps: Check OOM events: kubectl get events --field-selector reason=OOMKilling
Review memory usage: kubectl top pods -n namespace
Check pod resource limits: kubectl describe pod pod-name
Review logs before OOM: kubectl logs --previous pod-name
Increase memory limits temporarily in deployment manifest
Investigate memory leak using profiling tools

title: API Rate Limiting Configuration Guide
content: Rate limiting misconfigurations can cause legitimate traffic to be blocked. Always test rate limit changes in staging. Use graduated limits (warn at 80%, block at 100%). Monitor for false positive rejections.
steps: Review current rate limit config in API gateway admin console
Check recent 429 error rates in monitoring dashboard
Verify per-user vs per-IP limits are correct
Temporarily increase limits if blocking legitimate traffic
Test new limits in staging environment first
Set up alerts for 429 rate exceeding 1% of total requests

title: Kafka Consumer Lag Troubleshooting
content: High consumer lag indicates consumers cannot keep up with producers. Investigate consumer health, partition count, and processing rate. Consider scaling consumers or increasing partition count. Check for processing errors causing reprocessing loops.
steps: Check consumer lag: kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe --group group-id
Identify lagging partitions and check consumer health
Review consumer logs for errors or slow processing
Scale consumer instances if processing is too slow
Check for poison messages causing processing failures
Consider increasing partition count for parallelism

title: Load Balancer Health Check Configuration
content: Incorrect health check configuration can mark healthy instances as unhealthy, reducing capacity. Ensure health check endpoints return 200 OK and respond within the timeout. Test health checks manually.
steps: Check load balancer backend pool status in admin console
Manually test health endpoint: curl -f http://instance-ip/health
Review health check timeout and interval settings
Check application logs on marked-unhealthy instances
Adjust timeout if health endpoint is slow
Re-enable healthy instances after fixing root cause

title: Authentication Service Debugging Guide
content: Authentication issues can stem from Redis unavailability, JWT configuration issues, or session store problems. Check Redis connectivity first. Verify JWT secret consistency across service instances. Monitor token validation error rates.
steps: Check Redis connectivity: redis-cli -h redis-host ping
Review auth service error logs for specific failure types
Check Redis memory usage and eviction policy
Verify JWT_SECRET is consistent across all auth service pods
Check session TTL configuration
Restart auth service pods if Redis was recovered

title: CDN Cache Invalidation Runbook
content: After deployments, CDN cache must be invalidated to serve new assets. Automate this as part of the deployment pipeline. Verify CDN API credentials are fresh. Always confirm invalidation completed before marking deployment done.
steps: Check CDN API token is valid
Trigger cache invalidation via CDN dashboard or API
Monitor invalidation job status in CDN admin console
Test that new assets are being served
Check cache-control headers for proper max-age settings
Update deployment checklist to include cache invalidation step

title: Database Query Performance Optimization
content: Slow queries are a common cause of service latency. Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE to identify problematic queries. Add appropriate indexes. Avoid N+1 queries. Consider read replicas for reporting queries.
steps: Identify slow queries via pg_stat_statements
Analyze slow query: EXPLAIN ANALYZE your-query
Add missing indexes based on query plan
Consider partial indexes for filtered queries
Move expensive reports to read replica
Set statement_timeout for API queries

title: Disk Space Management for Build Servers
content: Build servers accumulate docker images, build artifacts, and logs over time. Set up automated cleanup. Monitor disk usage and alert at 80%.
steps: Check disk usage: df -h
Clean Docker resources: docker system prune -af --volumes
Remove old build artifacts: find /builds -mtime +7 -delete
Set up automated cleanup cron job
Expand disk or move to larger storage if needed
Set up alerting for disk usage over 80%

title: ETL Pipeline Failure Recovery
content: ETL failures require identifying the failure point and safely re-running from that point. Always ensure idempotency in ETL jobs. Use checkpointing to avoid full reruns.
steps: Review ETL job logs for failure point and error message
Check source system availability
Verify target data warehouse connectivity
Identify last successful checkpoint
Re-run ETL from last checkpoint (not full restart)
Validate data completeness after recovery

title: Mobile Push Notification Debugging
content: Push notification failures are often caused by expired certificates (APNS), invalid tokens, or FCM configuration issues. Check provider-specific dashboards for delivery rates.
steps: Check APNS certificate expiry for iOS push
Verify FCM API key validity for Android push
Check notification provider dashboard for delivery rates
Test with a known working device to isolate scope
Review device token registration freshness
Check payload size limits

title: Incident Response Runbook - P1 Critical
content: P1 Critical incidents require immediate response. Declare incident, assign roles (Incident Commander, Communications Lead, Technical Lead). Provide updates every 15 minutes. Focus on restoration over root cause during active incident.
steps: Declare incident in #incidents Slack channel
Page on-call engineer via PagerDuty
Assign Incident Commander (IC) role
Create incident bridge/war room
Identify customer impact and communicate to stakeholders
Focus on immediate mitigation and restoration
Provide status updates every 15 minutes
Escalate to engineering leadership if unresolved in 30 minutes
Post resolution: update status page
Schedule post-mortem within 48 hours

title: Service Health Check Implementation Guide
content: Every service must expose a /health endpoint. Implement shallow and deep health checks. Shallow: returns 200 if service is running. Deep: checks DB connectivity, cache availability, and upstream dependencies.
steps: Implement GET /health returning status: ok
Implement GET /health/deep checking DB, cache, and upstream services
Configure Kubernetes liveness probe on /health
Configure Kubernetes readiness probe on /health/deep
Set appropriate timeout and failure thresholds
Add health check to monitoring dashboard
